claims.text: A multiscale framework combining electronic-structure calculations with machine-learning defect corrections will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed approach will be effective in both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes.
The proposed approach applies to HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
As-cast bulk HfNbTaTiZr naturally contains defects.
The modeling framework will explicitly represent the effects of oxygen contamination and other defects on charge transport.
Oxygen and other microstructural imperfections alter local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen and other microstructural imperfections alter electron-phonon scattering mechanisms in HfNbTaTiZr.
A machine-learning module can learn the relationship between defect distributions and conduction behavior from lower-order calculations or experimental benchmarks.
The learned relationship can correct conductivity predictions generated from a perfect-crystal baseline.
Defect-driven variations in electron-scattering rates dominate conductivity behavior over the specified temperature regimes.
The hybrid model will have substantially smaller conductivity-prediction errors than standard analytical approaches.
At approximately 500 K, the hybrid model will improve prediction accuracy for the 1 wt.% oxygen sample by about 10–20% relative to a perfect-crystal prediction.
Conventional analytical conductivity models underpredict the effects of oxygen-induced scattering and other defects.
The claimed accuracy improvement is limited to roughly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Model accuracy may diminish outside the specified temperature ranges or at substantially higher impurity concentrations.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant error reduction of approximately 10–20% relative to the conventional model would falsify the hypothesis.
